lines: We compare 2023 ($N = 1{,}080$) against 2024 ($N = 807$) models; 31.3\% of items receive ETS~C classification ($|\Delta_{\mathrm{MH}}| \geq 1.5$; bootstrap 95\% CI: $[29.2\%, 37.8\%]$; family-level cluster bootstrap: $[26.7\%, 53.2\%]$, upper bound driven by mega-family over-representation; \Cref{app:uncertainty}). Two design-effect (DEFF) estimators bound the non-independence effect: simple-mean DEFF yields 29.2\% and weighted-mean DEFF yields 13.5\%, bracketing temporal C\% at 13.5--29.2\%. The cluster bootstrap 95\% CI ($[26.7\%, 53.2\%]$)---a family-level resampling method independent of DEFF methodology---excludes the weighted-mean estimate (13.5\%), providing model-independent evidence that over-correction drives the lower bound. Under weighted-mean DEFF (C\% $= 13.5\%$), all downstream conclusions hold: $\rho = 0.999$, score shift $= {+}1.77$\,pp (\Cref{app:deff}). Under 100 random permutations within the 2023 cohort (540 vs.\ 540), the 99th percentile of item-level $|\Delta_{\mathrm{MH}}|$ is 1.45---just below the ETS~C threshold of 1.5---confirming that the threshold maintains a per-item false-positive rate below 1\%; together with the Monte Carlo power analysis (TPR $\geq 0.68$; \Cref{sec:validation}), this validates ETS~C classification for the LLM setting. No non-dominant family drives the signal (LOFO $|\Delta\mathrm{C\%}| \leq 2.93$\,pp for families ${\leq}15\%$ of cohort; dominant-family drops reflect composition, not signal; \Cref{tab:lofo}); graduated de-duplication confirms C\% scales with power, not redundancy (\Cref{app:dedup_k}).
\looseness=-1

-Three controls confirm genuine temporal change (\Cref{tab:temporal_landscape}): random splits yield mean C\% of 0.62\% (2023; 100 permutations) and 1.3\% (2024; 100 permutations), both ${\geq}24\times$ below temporal C\%; ability-quintile comparison yields 2.9\%; and 1:1 nearest-neighbor matching on total score ($N{=}638$/group, Cohen's $d = -0.17$) yields C\% $= 28.9\% \pm 0.1\%$, confirming at most ${\sim}2.4$~pp is attributable to ability mismatch ($p < 0.01$; \Cref{app:method_details}).

\looseness=-1

Across all 57 subjects, C\% ranges from 20.7\% to 48.4\% (mean $\approx 30\%$; \Cref{tab:temporal_landscape}). DIF rates are domain-invariant (Kruskal-Wallis $p = 0.78$), but DIF \emph{direction} exhibits domain dependence: STEM items favor 2024 models (55.4\%), Humanities favor 2023 (64.4\%). DIF is item-specific: domain-level accuracy gains explain ${<}0.1\%$ of item-level DIF variance (\Cref{app:structural}). A difficulty--direction interaction emerges ($\rho = -0.597$): 2024 models gain on hard items while eroding on easy ones. The temporal DIF finding persists across thresholds ($18.4\%$ at $|\Delta_{\mathrm{MH}}| \geq 2.0$, $10.2\%$ at $\geq 2.5$).
